items.text: Houseplant hacks: should you water plants less in winter?
items.article: Don’t water based on the month or the season – be led by what the plant is actually doing The problem Cutting back on watering for winter has become so ingrained that people start rationing by the calendar, giving plants just a fraction of the water they had in summer, because the season changed. The hack The advice to reduce is because, as light levels drop, most houseplants slow their growth, use less water and dry out more slowly, so watering as you did in summer risks waterlogging the roots and causing rot. The method When we get to October, reduce watering to half or a quarter of what you gave plants in the summer. The test I reduced watering in two of my own plants last winter. A calathea in a cooler, dimmer room dried out more slowly and needed less watering, exactly as the hack predicts. But a pothos sitting under a grow light in a warm room kept growing and started crisping at the edges and dropping yellow leaves. The verdict The winter watering rule is not a myth, but it is badly misunderstood. The key is to water according to what the plant is doing, not what the calendar says. Research your plant to see if it has a dormant season and check each plant before you water. items.article: Martin Ott said one of his biggest takeaways from working under Zuckerberg was learning how to use limited time effectively rather than trying to fill every available hour with work. Martin Ott, a former Meta executive who worked with Mark Zuckerberg during Facebook’s years of rapid expansion, says his time at the company taught him an important lesson about productivity: working longer does not necessarily mean getting more done. Ott, who is now the CEO of Berlin-based tax platform Taxfix, joined Facebook in 2012 as managing director for Northern and Central Europe. The company was still privately held at the time, shifting from desktop to mobile and had only a few thousand employees worldwide. Speaking to Fortune , Ott said one of his biggest takeaways from working under Zuckerberg was learning how to use limited time effectively rather than trying to fill every available hour with work. “There’s only so many hours in a day,” Ott said. Instead of trying to tackle everything, Ott believes leaders should identify the task that could have the greatest impact on a particular day. He also suggested being more selective about meetings and asking whether attending each one is actually necessary. “Ask yourself, what is the real one thing you could do today to really have impact, make a difference?” he said.

It is a strategy. They quickly learn which parent is more likely to say yes, who is easier to persuade, who feels guilty more easily, and who might change their mind after enough pleading. A child asks one parent for permission to go to a party and is told no. Five minutes later, the same question is taken to the other parent, who says yes. Sometimes it is innocent. Sometimes it is deliberate. And sometimes the parents themselves are unaware of how often this happens. Parenting does not come with a handbook that tells two people how to agree on every decision. One parent may be stricter about screen time, while the other thinks an extra hour is harmless. One may believe that a teenager should be home by 7 pm, while the other says, “They are growing up, let them have some freedom.” One parent may insist that homework comes before play, while the other thinks the child has worked hard enough for the day. Differences are normal. In fact, they can be healthy. Children benefit from seeing that adults can think differently, negotiate, and still respect each other. items.article: The alleged attack on a Flydubai captain by his co-pilot has renewed focus on a cockpit safety rule shaped by two deadly aviation disasters. The alleged attack by a co-pilot on the captain of a Flydubai flight has once again brought into focus one of aviation’s most difficult security questions: what happens when the threat comes not from a passenger trying to enter the cockpit, but from someone already inside it? The question has confronted aviation regulators before. Two deadly crashes , separated by more than 15 years, became central to the debate over the danger posed by a pilot left alone at the controls — EgyptAir Flight 990 in 1999 and Germanwings Flight 9525 in 2015. On October 31, 1999, EgyptAir Flight 990 took off from New York’s John F Kennedy International Airport for Cairo with 203 passengers and 14 crew members aboard. The Boeing 767 was cruising at about 33,000 feet when Captain Ahmed El-Habashi left the cockpit to go to the toilet. Relief first officer Gameel Al-Batouti was left at the controls. What happened over the next few minutes became the subject of a bitter dispute between American and Egyptian investigators. According to the US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), Al-Batouti repeatedly said an Arabic phrase translated as “I rely on God". Less than a minute later, the autopilot was disconnected, and the aircraft began a steep descent.

A smart light can offer sixteen million colours, voice control and automation. items.text: Do We Actually Need a Smartwatch?
items.article: I still wear an analogue watch quite often. It doesn’t know how many steps I’ve taken, how well I slept or whether I’m stressed. It has never congratulated me for standing up, and it certainly doesn’t vibrate because somebody has sent “Good Morning" to a WhatsApp group. But smartwatches are everywhere now, which makes me wonder: do we actually need them, or have we simply become used to having another screen attached to our bodies? From what I see around me, most people wearing smartwatches aren’t studying HRV, recovery scores or detailed health trends. Many probably couldn’t tell you what half those measurements mean. What almost everybody understands is one wonderfully simple number: Somewhere along the way, walking became a competitive sport. The watch says 9,643 steps at 10.30 at night and suddenly somebody is pacing around the bedroom because apparently going to sleep with 357 steps outstanding would be an admission of defeat.
